title: Edge cases first
objectives: List edge cases and write tests before the solution.

screens.title: Which inputs catch the bug
screens.prose: `longest_streak(xs)` is the length of the longest run of equal neighbours: `[1, 1, 2, 2, 2]` gives 3. This version, m1, has a planted bug. The usual edge cases are empty, one and many, and random lists miss them. New here: a bug marks your tests.

params.title: Version m1 of longest_streak
lines: best = run = 0
for i, x in enumerate(xs):
if i and x == xs[i - 1]:
run += 1
else:
best = max(best, run)
run = 1
return best

hints.text: Where does m1 record the length of a run?
It records at a break, in the `else` branch.
A run that reaches the end of the list never meets a break. So the answer must be a run at the end.

feedback.correct: The last run is the longest in `[2, 2, 2]` and `[3, 1, 1]`, so m1 misses it.

screens.title: Write the tests
screens.prose: Six wrong versions are hidden. Return at most 8 inputs that tell every one of them apart from the correct function. The empty list is `[]`.

params.title: The six wrong versions
lines: m1 forgets the last run.
m2 returns 1 for an empty list.
m3 returns 0 for a single number.
m4 counts runs that never fall, so 1, 2 counts as a run.

m6 compares every number only with the first one.

screens.question: Write `edge_cases()`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Six ask whether one wrong version gives a different answer on one of your inputs. The seventh needs at most 8 lists of whole numbers.

hints.text: Which bugs does the empty list catch? And a single number?
`[]` catches m2 and `[7]` catches m1 and m3.
Add `[1, 2]` for m4 and `[3, 1, 1]` for m5 and m6. `[1, 1, 2, 2, 2]` catches four at once.

feedback.correct: These six inputs catch all six wrong versions.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which test failed.

byKey.test-1: Test 1: m1 forgets the last run. Add a list that ends on its longest run.
byKey.test-2: Test 2: m2 gives 1 for an empty list. Add `[]`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3: m3 gives 0 for one number. Add a one-element list.
byKey.test-4: Test 4: m4 counts runs that never fall. Add a list with a rise, such as `[1, 2]`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: m5 restarts at 0 after a break. Add a run after a break that is longer than the first run, such as `[3, 1, 1]`.

explain.text: Each input exposes the wrong versions whose answers differ from the correct one. `[]` and `[7]` take the two length cases, and `[1, 2]` takes the rise. `[3, 1, 1]` and `[1, 1, 2, 2, 2]` take the runs after a break.

m4, which counts runs that never fall
options.why: You thought m4 would hide. A random list has many rises, and each one makes m4 count too much.

options.text: m5, which restarts a run at 0 after a break
options.why: You chose a bug that shows whenever a run after a break is longer than the first run. Most random lists of 5 or more hold such a run.

Five numbers. It never makes an empty list.
m2 differs from the correct version only on `[]`, so only a list of length 0 catches it.

feedback.correct: Every random list has at least 5 numbers, so the empty list never appears.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which bug needs a list the loop never makes?

byKey.b: A list of 5 or more numbers with one rise already exposes m4.
byKey.c: A random list with a run after a break that is longer than the first run exposes m5.
byKey.d: A random list where another value's run beats every run of the first value exposes m6.

explain.text: The loop makes lists of length 5 to 50, so it never makes the empty list. m2 differs from the correct version only there. Random tests do not replace the empty, single and repeated cases.

screens.title: The same game in C++
screens.prose: `TEST(name) { ... }` runs a test and `CHECK(cond)` fails it when `cond` is false. Write `TEST` blocks with `CHECK`. A hidden `longest_streak` and five planted bugs, `BUG1` to `BUG5`, are the same as m1 to m5. The starter catches only `BUG2`.

params.title: testkit in C++
lines: TEST(name) { CHECK(condition); } registers a test.
run_tests() returns how many tests failed.
The hidden function has five bugs, switched on one at a time.

screens.question: Write tests that fail on every bug and pass on the correct version.

widget.how: Check runs 6 cases. Your tests must all pass the correct function, and each of five planted bugs must make a test fail.

hints.text: Your starter catches only the empty list. What else do the bugs need?
Add a single number, a rise, a run after a break and a run that fills the list.
Use `{7}`, `{1, 2}`, `{3, 1, 1}`, `{2, 2, 2}` and `{1, 1, 2, 2, 2}`, each with the expected value worked out by hand.

feedback.correct: All six checks pass: your tests accept the correct version and fail every bug.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which case failed.

byKey.test-2: Test 2: BUG1 passed your tests. Add a list that ends on its longest run.
byKey.test-3: Test 3: BUG2 passed your tests. Check the empty-list test.
byKey.test-4: Test 4: BUG3 passed your tests. Add a one-element list.

screens.title: Edge cases by family
screens.prose: Edge inputs come in families: strings, then intervals, then numbers. For each call, work out the answer.

params.title: Three small functions
lines: longest_run(s): the longest run of one letter in a string.
blocks(spans): how many blocks the closed intervals merge into.
digits(n): how many digits the whole number n has, ignoring its sign.

screens.question: Fill in the expected value of each call.

hints.text: Each call is the edge of its family: empty, touching, nested, zero, negative.
Closed intervals that share an end join into one block.
`[3, 4]` lies inside `[1, 9]`, so one block. Zero has one digit, and the sign is not a digit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what the edge input does.

byKey.r0c1: An empty string has no letters and no run, so 0.
byKey.r1c1: Three equal letters are one run of 3.
byKey.r2c1: Closed intervals that touch at 2 join, so one block.
byKey.r4c1: Zero is written with one digit.

explain.text: Each row is the edge of one family. The empty string, touching and nested intervals, and zero and negatives are where solutions slip. Write them before the code, with answers worked out by hand.

screens.question: Put the test-first steps in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: List the empty, single, repeated and boundary inputs
Write each expected output by hand
Write a stub that returns a wrong value
Run the tests and watch them fail
Write the solution, then pick tests it passes
lines.why: Then the solution picks the tests, so they cannot catch its own mistakes.

hints.text: Why watch the tests fail?
A test that cannot fail proves nothing.
List the inputs and expected outputs, then run them on a stub to see them fail. Write the real code and see them pass.

feedback.correct: List, expect, stub, fail, solve, pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The tests come before the solution.

byKey.d1: You let the solution choose the tests. Tests written after the code tend to pass it.
byKey.left-out: Six steps belong. Only picking tests after the solution is wrong.
byKey.t5: The real solution comes after the tests have failed on the stub.

explain.text: The inputs and their expected outputs fix what right means. A stub shows the tests can fail, and only then do we write the solution. A second run shows that it passes.

hints.text: Where do interval solutions slip?
At the ends: empty, touching and nested.
Choose the empty list, the touching pair and the nested pair. The spread-out inputs pass almost any code.

feedback.correct: The empty list, the touching pair and the nested pair.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the three edges, not the ordinary inputs.

screens.prose: Ten candidate inputs: `[]`, `[7]`, `[1, 2]`, `[3, 1, 1]`, `[2, 2, 2]`, `[1, 1, 2, 2, 2]`, `[1, 1]`, `[2, 1]`, `[1, 2, 2]` and `[6, 6, 6, 1]`. Choose the fewest that expose all six wrong versions.

`[]` catches m2 and `[7]` catches m1 and m3.
`[1, 1, 2, 2, 2]` catches m1, m4, m5 and m6. Together the three expose all six.

That you have a method for the inputs that break code.

Run the tests on a wrong version first. A test that cannot fail proves nothing.

quiz.question: Why can random tests miss a bug?

options.text: They seldom make cases such as the empty list
They repeat the same list again and again
options.why: You thought random lists repeat. They differ each time, but they share a typical shape.

options.text: They are too slow to run on large inputs
options.why: Speed is not the problem. A million lists run quickly and still miss the empty list.

options.text: They only find bugs in the last run of a list
options.why: You tied random tests to one bug. Their weakness is the special case.

feedback.correct: Random lists have a typical shape, so special cases are rare or absent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what a random list looks like.

byKey.b: Random lists differ, but none of them is special.
byKey.c: Running time is not the issue.
byKey.d: No bug is tied to the last run only.

explain.text: Random lists are typical lists. The empty list, one number and an all-equal list are special, and a generator seldom makes them.

quiz.question: You write tests for a function that reverses a string. Which input family do you add first?

options.text: The empty string and one letter
The longest string you can build
options.why: You chose size first. Short inputs expose more slips than long ones.

options.text: A string with every letter of the alphabet
options.why: You chose a rich string. Rich strings pass a lot of broken code.

options.text: A string copied from the statement
options.why: You chose the example. The example is the case the setter knew would work.

feedback.correct: The empty string and one letter come first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the smallest inputs.

byKey.b: Large inputs test speed, not the edge.
byKey.c: A rich string rarely exposes a slip.
byKey.d: The example in the statement passes most attempts.

explain.text: Empty and one-letter inputs are where loops and indexes slip. They go first, before the larger cases.
